summary: UAP over Harare airport recorded on radar AND optical. Hovers at undetermined altitude with beams emanating. Released in PURSUE Tranche 3.
what: In July 2008, a UAP was recorded over Harare International Airport via both radar and optical systems. The object was reported to hover at an undetermined altitude with beams emanating from it. The case surfaced in a CIA/FBI-stream document released in PURSUE Tranche 3 (June 12, 2026).
why: Dual-sensor (radar + optical) attestation from an African capital — a region nearly absent from official corpora until 2026. Beam emission matches Colares 1977 phenomenology. Zimbabwe now appears twice in the record via independent channels: the 1994 Ariel School mass child-witness case (Ruwa) and this 2008 instrumented case, 14 years apart.
witnesses: Airport radar operators and optical observers (identities redacted in release).
evidence: PURSUE Tranche 3 document (CIA/FBI stream), June 12, 2026. Radar + optical dual-sensor record.
response: No known Zimbabwean government investigation disclosed. US IC filed and retained the report; declassified 18 years later.

sensors.note: Dual-sensor radar+optical success

name: Genkai Nuclear Plant Lights
location: Genkai Nuclear Power Plant, Saga, Japan
summary: Three lights hover 2+ hours over operating nuclear plant. Regulator retracts drone ID next day: only lights that appeared to be drones. Closed Diet hearings follow.
what: On July 26, 2025, four security guards and a stationed police officer witnessed three lights resembling drones hovering for over two hours above Kyushu Electric's Genkai Nuclear Power Plant (No. 3 reactor operational). The lights vanished by early morning. No drone was recovered and no operator identified. Japan's Nuclear Regulation Authority initially announced three drones, then corrected itself the next day: only lights that appeared to be drones — it could not be said with certainty they were drones.
why: A fresh 2025 data point in the nuclear-facility pattern (Malmstrom, Usovo, Rendlesham, PANTEX) — multi-witness, multi-hour, with an official regulatory retraction from identification to non-identification. On August 7, 2025, Japan's Parliamentary UAP League held closed-door hearings taking testimony from the NRA, Defense Ministry, and Land Ministry.
witnesses: 4 security guards + 1 police officer. Multi-hour continuous observation.
evidence: NRA public correction (July 27, 2025). Kyushu Electric report to regulator. Asahi Shimbun reporting on closed hearings (Sept 4, 2025).
response: NRA correction issued. Closed Diet hearings Aug 7, 2025. Feeds the March 2026 proposal for a UAP body under the Deputy Chief Cabinet Secretary.

sensors.note: 2+hrs multi-witness; no usable imagery/ID; nothing recovered

name: Lake Huron Shootdown
summary: First-ever released footage of US military kinetic engagement against a UAP-designated object. AIM-9X strike fragments object in radial high-energy pattern. Debris fate undisclosed.
what: On February 12, 2023 — one week after the Chinese balloon shootdown — an Air National Guard F-16C engaged an unidentified object over Lake Huron with an AIM-9X Sidewinder. The 46-second Advanced Targeting Pod infrared video, released in PURSUE Tranche 2 (May 22, 2026), shows the object struck and fragmenting in a radial displacement pattern DoW language calls suggestive of a high-energy event. Fragments visibly fall.
why: Historic as the first visual record of a US kinetic UAP engagement, regardless of the object's ultimate identity. November 2024 documents point to hobbyist/weather-balloon debris; the government has not disclosed what fell or whether recovery was attempted. Released only after congressional pressure routed through AARO.
witnesses: F-16 pilots (callsigns redacted). NORAD radar operators.
evidence: Official DoW ATP infrared video (PURSUE Tranche 2). Prior NORAD statements. 2024 debris-vendor documents (balloon hypothesis).
response: Object engaged and destroyed. Recovery status undisclosed. Footage classified 3 years, released May 22, 2026.

sensors.note: Full kill chain worked (1st missile missed); debris fate undisclosed

name: Ladakh Luminous Objects
summary: 100+ Unidentified Luminous Objects logged by ITBP and Army over 2.5 months at the India-China line. ISRO, DRDO, NTRO all investigated — all failed to identify. Drones and satellites formally ruled out.
what: Between August 1 and October 15, 2012, the ITBP unit at Thakung near Pangong Tso reported over 100 sightings of yellowish luminous spheres rising from the horizon on the Chinese side, gliding across the sky for three to four hours before vanishing. The Army documented 99 sightings January–August across Ladakh sectors. A drone was sent up and a radar deployed; the objects were not identified. Army, ISRO, DRDO and NTRO investigations all failed; UAVs, Chinese drones and low-orbit satellites were formally excluded.
why: The largest documented multi-agency identification failure in the world, at a nuclear-armed contested border, sustained over months — anchor case of the contested-border luminous-orb pattern. A 1968 declassified CIA document records six sightings over the same terrain, a five-decade thread.
witnesses: ITBP border police units, Indian Army 14 Corps personnel; multi-observer, multi-week.
evidence: ITBP photographs studied at Army HQ; 14 Corps detailed report; press documentation (India Today, The Hindu). No public sensor data released.
response: File sent to Army HQ; investigations closed without identification; no public policy response; no Indian UAP body exists.

name: La Joya AFB Engagement
location: La Joya Air Base, Arequipa, Peru
summary: FAP pilot Oscar Santa María Huertas fired ~64 rounds of 30mm cannon at a balloon-like object that then outran his Su-22 to 19 km altitude. Documented in a declassified US DoD record.
what: On April 11, 1980, ordered to intercept a stationary object over La Joya's restricted airspace, Lt. Santa María fired a burst of 30mm shells at close range with no visible effect. The object then ascended and outmaneuvered the Su-22 through a 22-minute pursuit to ~63,000 ft, repeatedly stopping and evading firing solutions. Up close he described a ~10m dome with a wide silver base, no engines, no exhaust.
why: One of very few documented cases of a military pilot firing on a UAP — recorded in a June 1980 US Department of Defense document ('UFO Sighted in Peru') and testified publicly by the pilot in 2013. Anchors Peru's OIFAA institutional file.
witnesses: Lt. Oscar Santa María Huertas (pilot, on-record to present day); base personnel (~1,800 on the ground).
evidence: Declassified US DoD document, June 1980; pilot testimony, Citizen Hearing 2013.
response: Peru later created/reactivated OIFAA under FAP aerospace directorate (2001/2013).

name: Aguadilla Transmedium Object
location: Rafael Hernández Airport, Aguadilla, Puerto Rico
summary: DHS/CBP aircraft thermal video: object crosses the airfield, repeatedly enters and exits the ocean without deceleration, appears to split in two. Subject of a 161-page SCU analysis.
what: On April 25, 2013 (~21:20 local), a DHS Customs and Border Protection DHC-8's thermal imager tracked a small fast object over the airport and coastline; the footage shows repeated ocean entry and exit with no deceleration signature and an apparent split into two objects near the end of the track. Airport radar had a correlating intermittent primary return; commercial departure was delayed during the event.
why: The Caribbean anchor of the transmedium ledger and among the strongest sensor-video transmedium records in open circulation — a federal law-enforcement platform, chain-of-custody known, analyzed at length by the Scientific Coalition for UAP Studies.
witnesses: CBP aircrew; tower personnel.
evidence: CBP thermal video (leaked, authenticity undisputed); SCU 161-page technical analysis; radar correlation.
response: No official DHS analysis released; case remains formally unresolved.

name: Petrozavodsk Phenomenon
summary: A vast 'jellyfish' of light over northwest USSR, mass-witnessed and reported in Pravda — the event that forced the Soviet state to create the 13-year SETKA program.
what: Early on September 20, 1977, a brilliant expanding luminous 'jellyfish' display was observed across Karelia and neighboring regions, showering ray-like filaments; reported by TASS and covered in Pravda/Izvestiya, generating 1,500+ citizen letters to the Academy of Sciences.
why: The institutional trigger case of the Eastern bloc: within a year the Military-Industrial Commission ordered SETKA-MO and SETKA-AN into the state plan. Retrospective analyses associate the display with the Kosmos-955 launch from Plesetsk — a substantially explained case retained for its institutional consequence and as a calibration exhibit.
witnesses: Mass civilian + officials across multiple cities.
evidence: Contemporary Soviet press; Academy correspondence; program documents sold post-1991.
response: Creation of SETKA (1978–1990), the largest systematic sky-watch ever ordered.

name: Pantex Plant Lockdown Pursuit
location: Pantex Nuclear Weapons Plant, Amarillo, Texas
summary: Sept 1, 2015: America's nuclear weapons assembly plant went into LOCKDOWN as security officers pursued a completely silent, slow-moving diamond-shaped object with no visible propulsion. Released as DOE-UAP-D005, PURSUE Tranche 4.
what: Security personnel observed a diamond-shaped object — rounded at top, roughly four feet tall and two feet wide at the base, described variously as black or silver/red/blue — traveling at only 10–15 mph over the facility. The plant was placed on lockdown; two officers pursued by vehicle, then exited and assessed the object through binoculars: no sound whatsoever, no identifiable propulsion system. After 1–2 minutes of observation it continued north offsite.
why: Second Pantex file in the official record (with the Tranche 2 DOE file) and the modern bookend of the nuclear-facility thread the vault now anchors at both ends: the 1949 Los Alamos conference (DOC-004) to Pantex 2015 — 66 years. Slow, silent, propulsion-less flight over the most sensitive weapons facility in America, officially unresolved.
witnesses: Multiple Pantex security officers (binocular assessment on record).
evidence: DOE incident report DOE-UAP-D005 (war.gov Tranche 4, July 10, 2026). No sensor imagery released.
response: Facility lockdown; pursuit; report filed to DOE; released under PURSUE July 2026.

name: Yellow Sea Sensor-Degradation UAP
summary: Official Department of War release describing a UAP that progressively degraded electro-optical and infrared sensor footage over 4 minutes 57 seconds — the first official case to describe degradation occurring during observation.
what: Across a 4:57 engagement, an unidentified object over the Yellow Sea appeared to progressively degrade the capturing platform's electro-optical and infrared sensor footage. The effect worsened as the observation continued rather than resolving, which is atypical of ordinary lock-loss or range effects. Released in the DOW-UAP-PR104/105 family.
why: If the degradation is a property of the object or its interaction with the sensor (rather than an artifact), it would be a rare instance of an observation-time counter-sensor effect on record in official material — the kind of signature that separates a genuine unknown from a mundane misidentification.
witnesses: Sensor-operator crew of the capturing platform; footage reviewed by the Department of War / AARO-successor office.
evidence: Official DoW release (DOW-UAP-PR104/105 family): 4:57 of IR footage showing progressive degradation during observation.
response: First official release describing sensor degradation during observation. CAVEAT: compression and atmospheric artifacts have not yet been excluded as alternative explanations.

sensors.note: Official DoW description: UAP 'appears to degrade electro-optical and infrared sensor footage' progressively over 4:57 (DOW-UAP-PR104/105 family). First official release describing degradation-during-observation. CAVEAT: compression/atmospheric artifacts not yet excluded.

name: Dalnegorsk — Height 611
summary: On 29 Jan 1986 a reddish sphere flew level and struck the hill 'Height 611' near Dalnegorsk. Recovered site material was studied by Soviet Academy of Sciences labs.
what: On 29 January 1986 a dull-red spherical object, roughly the size of a small car, flew in level, non-ballistic flight and struck a rocky hilltop (Height 611) near Dalnegorsk in the Soviet Far East. It burned on the hill in a series of flashes for close to an hour. Investigators later recovered scorched rock, tiny woven 'mesh' nets, and small glass and metallic spherules from the impact zone.
why: One of the best-documented physical-trace UAP cases from the Soviet Union: controlled non-ballistic flight, an energetic impact, and residue that underwent laboratory analysis — a rare combination of eyewitness and material evidence from a closed-archive country.
witnesses: Numerous Dalnegorsk townspeople watched the object and the hilltop glow; a formal investigation team examined the site over following weeks.
evidence: Physical residue — fine metallic mesh and glass/gold-bearing spherules — analysed by researchers linked to the USSR Academy of Sciences' Far-Eastern branch; scorched impact area.
response: Studied by Soviet scientists; no conventional explanation was established for the trajectory or the recovered material. Samples and findings remain debated.

name: Voronezh Park Landing
summary: In autumn 1989 residents and children in a Voronezh park reported a large sphere landing with tall occupants. TASS carried the story worldwide, drawing Western skepticism.
what: Over several weeks in September–October 1989, groups of residents — many of them children — in a park in Voronezh's Western District reported a large hovering sphere that touched down, leaving ground impressions, with accounts of tall figures nearby. The Soviet news agency TASS reported it as fact, and it was carried by international press.
why: Notable for the number and consistency of ordinary witnesses and, again, for open Soviet state reporting — a data point from a region and era that produced very little public UAP documentation.
witnesses: Multiple children and adults in the Western District; interviewed by local scientists and journalists.
evidence: TASS state dispatch (Oct 1989) carried by Reuters, AP and others; reported ground indentations at the park site.
response: Soviet researchers recorded witness testimony; Western outlets covered it with heavy skepticism. No agreed explanation.

name: Hangzhou Xiaoshan Airport Incident
summary: On 7 July 2010 an unidentified object over Hangzhou forced Xiaoshan International Airport to halt operations; flights were grounded and diverted for about four hours.
what: On the evening of 7 July 2010, an unidentified luminous object was seen and photographed over Hangzhou in eastern China. Xiaoshan International Airport suspended operations for roughly four hours, grounding and diverting flights while the object was tracked. Multiple residents captured photographs of a bright, streaking form.
why: A modern, aviation-disrupting case from China — a country almost entirely absent from Western UAP datasets — with hard operational consequences (an airport shutdown) and civilian imagery, making it unusually well-attested for the region.
witnesses: Airport staff, flight crews, and Hangzhou residents; several photographs entered the public record.
evidence: Airport closure and flight-diversion records; multiple civilian photographs; Xinhua and international news coverage.
response: Authorities indicated part of the airspace activity had a 'military-related' cause but released no specifics; the photographed object itself was never publicly explained.

name: China Airport UFO Wave
summary: Across 2010–2011 a series of unidentified objects disrupted Chinese airports (Xiaoshan, Baotou, Chongqing), grounding or diverting flights on several occasions.
what: Following the July 2010 Hangzhou event, China saw a run of similar airport-disrupting sightings into 2011, affecting airports including Baotou (Inner Mongolia) and Chongqing among others. Flights were grounded or rerouted while glowing objects were observed. Chinese and international media tracked the recurring pattern.
why: Aggregated, the wave shows the phenomenon repeatedly interacting with controlled airspace in China — a systemic signal from a closed-information environment, comparable in structure to the NJ drone wave or the Belgian wave elsewhere in this dataset.
witnesses: Airport personnel, pilots and passengers across several Chinese cities; extensive domestic (Xinhua) and foreign (Reuters, BBC) reporting.
evidence: Repeated airport closure/diversion records over ~a year; sustained state and international press coverage.
response: Authorities acknowledged the disruptions; explanations offered for individual events (e.g. test-flight debris) were not extended to the wave as a whole.

name: Ukraine Front-Line Drone Object
summary: A Ukrainian war drone filmed a round object with six lighted cones at ~800 m over the front line (May 2025). A senior Defence Ministry advisor published the footage in May 2026 — a rare official-adjacent wartime release.
what: During front-line drone operations in May 2025, a Ukrainian reconnaissance drone captured close-range video of a round object showing six lighted cones around a central illumination, at a reported altitude of about 800 meters. Serhiy Beskrestnov, senior advisor to Ukraine's Ministry of Defence on UAVs and electronic warfare, published the footage publicly in May 2026. The exact position remains undisclosed; the map point marks the approximate front sector.
why: An active war zone saturated with drones, EW sensors and constant optical coverage is a uniquely instrumented environment — and this release came through an official-adjacent military channel rather than a civilian leak. It also landed the same month as the first US PURSUE-era tranche, suggesting release pressure is now international.
witnesses: Ukrainian drone operators; footage reviewed and published by a senior MoD advisor.
evidence: Drone electro-optical video (close approach). Single-sensor: no radar, IR, or multi-platform corroboration has been published.
response: Published by the MoD advisor without official identification. Independent analysts have proposed prosaic explanations, including an out-of-focus optical artifact of a point light source; the interpretation remains contested. CAVEAT: single-sensor capture — treat as unresolved, not anomalous.
